text: Carlotta Gall is a British journalist and author who covered Afghanistan and Pakistan for The New York Times for twelve years and is currently covering the war in Ukraine. She is the daughter of veteran Scottish journalist Sandy Gall and began her newspaper career with The Moscow Times in Moscow in 1994, where she covered the first war in Chechnya extensively and reported on various events across the former Soviet Union. She also freelanced for British publications such as The Independent, The Times, and The Sunday Times, as well as American outlets including USA Today, Newsweek, and The New York Times. In 1996, she co-authored Chechnya: A Small Victorious War with Thomas de Waal; the following year, they published Chechnya: Calamity in the Caucasus, which won the James Cameron Prize for Distinguished Reporting in the UK. Gall received the Kurt Schork award for international freelance journalism in 2002, the Interaction award for international reporting in 2005, and the Edward Weintal Prize for diplomatic reporting from Georgetown University's Institute for the Study of Diplomacy in 2007. In 1998, she moved to the Financial Times and The Economist, reporting from Baku, Azerbaijan on the Caucasus and Central Asia. From 1999 to 2001, she worked in the Balkans for The New York Times, covering the wars in Kosovo, Serbia, and Macedonia, as well as developments in Bosnia and the rest of the former Yugoslavia. From 2001 to 2013, she served as a correspondent for The New York Times covering Pakistan and Afghanistan. From 2013 to 2017, she was the newspaper's North Africa correspondent based in Tunis and then became the Times' bureau chief in Istanbul, Turkey. Gall is featured in the Academy Award-winning documentary Taxi to the Dark Side (2007), where she was the first journalist to report on two Afghans who died in US custody at Bagram air base (Parwan Detention Facility); the documentary centers on the case of Afghan taxi driver Dilawar, who was beaten to death in 2002 while in US-military custody, with the military officially stating the cause of death was natural, but Gall uncovered what she considers incontrovertible evidence to the contrary. In 2014, in her book The Wrong Enemy: America in Afghanistan, 2001–2014, she accused Pakistan's clandestine intelligence service, the ISI, of hiding and protecting Osama bin Laden and his family after the September 11, 2001, attacks.
